The arising of worldly engagement is 'enjoyment' (bhoga) and the strengthening of renunciation is 'yoga'. The Gita believes that 'Everything is the Supreme Being' and emphasizes this very point. To demonstrate that 'I alone exist in all forms—as action, as cause, as glory, and in all manifestations', the Lord has described His divine glories (vibhutis) in four places in the Gita (in Chapters Seven, Nine, Ten, and Fifteen). Brahman (the formless, attributeless Supreme), kritsna adhyatma (all living beings across infinite species), akhila karma (all cosmic activities of creation, preservation, and dissolution), adhibhuta (the entire physical world made of the five elements, including one's own body), adhidaiva (all demigods including Brahma along with the presiding deities of the mind and senses), and adhiyajna (the inner dweller Vishnu and all His manifestations)—all of these are subsumed under 'vasudevah sarvam' (Vasudeva is everything) (Gita 7.29-30). The gist is that whatever is existent (sat), non-existent (asat), and beyond both is all the Supreme Being alone—'tvam aksaram sad asat tat param yat' (Gita 11.37). The world appears real only due to one's attachment (raga). It is because of attachment that a secondary existence appears. If attachment ceases, there is nothing except the one Supreme Being. As the Lord has stated—'sarvasya caham hridi sannivistah' (Gita 15.15), "I am seated in the hearts of all living beings." In the very heart where the Lord dwells, there also arise attachment-aversion, agitation, and restlessness. Happiness arises in the heart, and sorrow comes to the heart. During the churning of the ocean, both poison and nectar emerged from the same place. When Lord Shiva drank the poison, nectar appeared. Similarly, if attachment and aversion are eradicated, the Supreme Being manifests. In the hearts of saints and great souls, attachment and aversion do not remain; hence, the Supreme Lord dwells there.

'Everything is the Supreme Being'—this is meditation with open eyes. In this, there is no need to close the eyes (dhyana), no need to close the ears (nadanusandhana), nor any need to hold the breath (pranayama)! In this state, neither union nor separation has any effect; neither anyone's arrival nor anyone's departure makes any difference. When everything is the Supreme Being, where would another come from? How would they come?

The Gita accepts the integral Whole (Samagra); hence, the Gita begins and ends with surrender (sharanagati). Only through surrender is the Whole attained. Although all forms are included in the integral form of the Supreme Being, the personal/attributeful aspect (Saguna) holds prominence. This is because the unmanifest/attributeless aspect (Nirguna) is also contained within Saguna, but Saguna (owing to the negation of attributes in Nirguna) is not contained within Nirguna. Therefore, only Saguna can be the integral Whole. Lord Shri Krishna is integral—'asamsayam samagram mam' (Gita 7.1). The Gita is the voice of the Integral Whole, which is why everything is contained in the Gita. In whatever perspective one views the Gita, the Gita appears to them accordingly—'ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham' (Gita 4.11).

Karmayoga, Jnanayoga, and Bhaktiyoga—these are the only three Yogas. Karmayoga pertains to the body (Apara), Jnanayoga pertains to the indweller/Self (Para), and Bhaktiyoga pertains to the Master of both body and Self (the Lord). At the beginning of the Gita, the Lord first described Jnanayoga and Karmayoga respectively, taking up the indweller (Self) first and then the body. Then Dhyanayoga was described, because that is also a means of spiritual attainment. Then from the seventh chapter onwards, Bhakti was described with special emphasis, which is the Lord's primary objective. Through Karmayoga a person becomes useful to the world, through Jnanayoga for oneself, and through Bhaktiyoga for the Lord.

In the Gita, equanimity is called 'Yoga'—'samatvam yoga ucyate' (Gita 2.48). In reality, the need for 'Yoga' is only in action (karma); there is no need for yoga in knowledge, and in devotion, there is absolutely no need for yoga. Knowledge and devotion are themselves 'Yoga'. Actions are inert, binding, and sense-oriented; therefore, yoga is required in them—'yogasthah kuru karmani' (Gita 2.48). In actions, yoga is paramount—'yogah karmasu kaushalam' (Gita 2.50). Action without yoga is inferior—'durena hy avaram karma buddhiyogad dhananjaya' (Gita 2.49). Sense of agency (kartritva) also arises from performing actions. Therefore, in the Gita, the word 'Yoga' specifically denotes 'Karmayoga'. In the colophon (pushpika) of the Gita as well, the term 'Yogasastre' refers to the teachings of Karmayoga.

In Karmayoga, there are two divisions—the action division (Karma-vibhaga) and the yoga division (Yoga-vibhaga). The action division is the former half, and the yoga division is the latter half. Action depends on instruments (karana-sapeksh), whereas yoga is independent of instruments (karana-nirapeksh). The action division contains devotion to duty, while the yoga division contains freedom, changelessness, unattachment, and equanimity. What is our duty in the world is someone else's right. (4) In the instrument-dependent method, immediate attainment is never achieved; but in the instrument-independent method, upon completely severing connection with inert matter, abiding in one's true nature, or taking refuge in the Lord, immediate attainment is achieved.

|

In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, importance is given to the instrument-dependent method for the attainment of Yoga, whereas in the Gita, importance is given solely to the instrument-independent method for the attainment of Yoga. If the mind becomes fixed on the Supreme, that is fine; but if the mind is not fixed, nothing is achieved—this is the instrument-dependent method. Whether the mind is fixed on the Supreme or not makes no difference, provided one's inner self attaches directly to the Supreme—this is the instrument-independent method. The essence is that in the instrument-dependent method, the relation with the Supreme is via the mind and intellect, while in the instrument-independent method, one's inner self attaches directly to the Supreme by severing connection with the mind and intellect. Therefore, in the instrument-dependent method, attainment comes gradually through practice; but in the instrument-independent method, practice is not required. This is because one's relationship with the Supreme is an eternally established relationship (nitya-yoga). Hence, practice is not needed to accept or know one's relationship with God; just as after marriage, a woman accepts a man as her husband without having to perform any practice to accept it. Similarly, when someone points out, 'This is the sacred Ganga', no practice is required to know it. In the instrument-dependent method, primary emphasis is on performing spiritual practice (action) for oneself; but in the instrument-independent method, primary emphasis is on knowing (discrimination) and accepting (inner feeling).

Even when a seeker does not yet directly experience 'I have no relationship whatsoever with inert matter (body, etc.)', if they firmly accept this from the very beginning, they gain that very clear experience. Just as one was bound by holding the false belief 'I am the body and the body is mine', similarly one is liberated by holding the true belief 'I am not the body and the body is not mine'; because an assumed belief vanishes when it is no longer accepted—this is the principle. The Lord states this in the Gita: an ignorant person attaches himself to the body and considers himself the doer of actions arising from it—'ahankara-vimudhatma kartaham iti manyate' (Gita 3.27). But a wise person does not consider himself the doer of those actions—'naiva kincit karomit yukto manyeta tattvavit' (Gita 5.8). The implication is that to eliminate an unreal belief, it is essential to establish a real belief.

|

Beliefs such as 'I am a Hindu', 'I am a Brahmin', 'I am a renunciate' become so deeply rooted that unless one gives them up oneself, no one else can remove them. Likewise, beliefs like 'I am the body', 'I am the doer' become so firm that letting them go seems difficult to the seeker. However, since these worldly beliefs are unreal and false, they are not permanent, but destined to perish. In contrast, true beliefs like 'I am not the body', 'I belong to God' are real and true, and therefore never perish; rather, they are merely forgotten or turned away from. Thus, when a real belief becomes firm, it does not remain a mere belief, but transforms into direct realization (experience).

Although the instrument-dependent method is also described in the Gita (such as in Chapter 4, verses 24 to 30 and verse 34; Chapter 6, verses 10 to 28; Chapter 8, verses 8 to 16; and Chapter 15...

1- If direct attainment of the Supreme Reality were achieved through the instrument-dependent method (restraint of mental modifications), then the 'Vibhuti Pada' of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (which describes supernatural powers) would become redundant. The powers attained through the instrument-dependent method are actually obstacles to attaining the Supreme Reality. Even in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, those powers are acknowledged as obstacles—'te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah' (Yoga Sutra 3.37), meaning those (powers) are obstacles to Samadhi and are accomplishments only in worldly waking state (vyutthan); 'sthany-upanimantrane sanga-smayakaranampunaranista-prasangat' (Yoga Sutra 3.51), meaning when invited by the celestial deities of higher realms, one should neither feel attachment to those pleasures nor take pride in them, for doing so risks downfall.

2- In truth, no worldly illustration fully applies to accepting or knowing the Supreme Being. This is because in accepting or knowing the world, the mind and intellect remain active with us; but in accepting or knowing the Supreme Being, the mind and intellect do not accompany us—meaning the experience of the Supreme is realized by the Self directly, not through the mind and intellect. Secondly, knowing or accepting the world has a beginning and an end, but knowing or accepting the Supreme Being has no beginning and no end. This is because in reality, our (Self's) connection with the world does not exist at all, whereas our connection with the Supreme Being has existed eternally and will remain forever.

The instrument-independent method of spiritual discipline is equally useful for everyone, as it requires no special qualification or external circumstance. In this method, simply possessing an intense desire for attaining the Supreme causes immediate severance of connection with inert matter, realizing the eternally attained Supreme Reality. Just as darkness of countless years is destroyed instantly upon striking a single matchstick, similarly, no matter how ancient (spanning infinite births) one's connection with inert matter may be, it vanishes the moment an intense longing for attaining the Supreme arises. Therefore, intense longing is superior even to Samadhi achieved through instrument-dependence. Even in the highest absorption (nirvikalpa samadhi), there is a return to waking state (vyutthan) followed by worldly activity—meaning Samadhi also has a beginning and an end. As long as there is a beginning and an end, connection with inert matter persists. Once connection with inert matter is severed, spiritual practice has no beginning or end; rather, one experiences eternal union with the Supreme Lord.*

In truth, separation from the Supreme Lord has never occurred, nor is it ever possible. It is only due to assumed association with the world that separation from the Supreme Lord appears to exist. The moment a seeker after the Supreme Reality gives up assumed attachment to the world, they instantly experience eternal union and become permanently established in it.

*

The eternal union of the individual soul with the eternally attained Supreme Reality is self-evident; hence, its attainment does not depend on instruments. One merely needs to direct one's vision towards it, as expressed in Sri Ramcharitmanas—'sankara sahaja sarupu samhara' (1.58.4), meaning Lord Shiva composed Himself in His natural essential form, directing His vision towards it. A thing that is 'kept/remembered' is something that is already with us and merely requires a glance to recognize its presence. In the same way, mere turning of vision yields the experience of eternal union. However, owing to desires for worldly pleasures, hopes, and enjoyment, turning vision towards it and experiencing it seems difficult. As long as one's vision is directed towards worldly enjoyment and accumulation, a person lacks the power to look towards their true Self. Even if by some reason or special contemplation one's vision turns there, keeping it steady is extremely difficult, because the deep-rooted affection for perishable objects prevents one from comprehending the self-evident relationship with God; and even if comprehended, does not let it remain steady. But if an intense longing awakens—'How may that Supreme Reality be experienced?'—then this longing possesses the power to destroy all attachment to the world.

Karmayoga, Jnanayoga, and Bhaktiyoga as taught in the Gita are all three instrument-independent, meaning they occur through the Self. Actions and objects do not belong to oneself nor are they for oneself; rather, they belong to others and are meant for serving others; 'I am not the body and the body is not mine; I belong to God and God belongs to me'—such contemplation or conviction conducted through discrimination is not instrument-dependent (practice), because in this there is severance of connection from inert matter. Thus, in Karmayoga, detachment from inert matter happens naturally.

* As long as connection with inert matter remains, two states persist; because being mutable, inert nature is never uniform. Thus, both Samadhi (absorption) and Vyutthan (waking/activity) occur only due to connection with inert matter. Upon severing connection with inert matter, the 'Sahajavastha' (natural state) arises, which saints call 'Sahaja Samadhi'. From this state, there is never any return to delusion.

In offering oblations, there is renunciation of grains, ghee, etc.; in giving charity, there is renunciation of material goods; in performing austerity, there is renunciation of one's own comfort and enjoyment; in performing duty (karma), there is renunciation of selfishness and personal ease. Therefore, the word 'Yajna' signifies all scripturally ordained activities such as ritual sacrifice (havan), charity, and austerity.

There is a story in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: Prajapati Brahma, having created devas (gods), humans, and asuras (demons), imparted to them the single syllable 'Da' (द). Owing to the abundance of enjoyment available to gods, they understood 'Da' to mean 'Damyata' (exercise self-control). Due to the hoarding tendency among humans, they understood 'Da' to mean 'Datta' (give in charity). Because demons possessed a strong inclination toward violence and causing distress to others, they understood 'Da' to mean 'Dayadhvam' (be compassionate). Thus, the underlying intent of the instruction given to devas, humans, and demons alike was to act for the welfare of others. When rain clouds thunder 'Da, Da, Da...', even today it serves as a reminder of Brahma's instruction (control yourselves, donate, show mercy) regarding one's duties (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Chapter 5, Brahmana 2, Mantras 1–3).

'Why should we fall behind in fulfilling our duty?' Thinking thus, peacocks also began to call out. Hearing the peacocks' calls, the clouds thought: 'Why are peacocks calling today without hearing our thunder?' Learning the whole matter, the clouds thought: 'Why should we shrink back from our duty?' And they too began to thunder. Hearing the thundering clouds, Indra wondered what was happening. Upon learning that they were performing their duty, Indra thought: 'Why should I lag behind in performing my duty?' So thinking, Indra ordered the clouds to rain down.

'Yajnah karma-samudbhavah'—all scripturally prescribed secular and spiritual duties performed without desire for results are called 'Yajna'. For a brahmachari (celibate student), performing daily agnihotra is 'Yajna'. Similarly, cooking meals for the family is 'Yajna' for women*. If an expert in Ayurveda practices medicine solely for the welfare of people, that very practice becomes 'Yajna' for him. Likewise, a student can regard his studies and a merchant his trade as 'Yajna' (provided it is carried out selflessly for the benefit of others). Thus, all duty-bound actions performed in accordance with scriptural ordinances while respecting the boundaries of varna, ashrama, place, and time are of the nature of 'Yajna'. Whatever form Yajna takes, it is generated through action.

When physicians purify toxic substances such as arsenic or marking nut and administer them as medicine, those poisons become like nectar and cure severe diseases. Similarly, desires, mine-ness, attachment, partiality, inequality, selfishness, and pride act like poison within actions. Once this poisonous element is eliminated from actions, those actions become ambrosial and cure the great disease of the cycle of birth and death. Such ambrosial actions alone are called 'Yajna'.

How does performing one's duty lead to rainfall? Example and action naturally have a greater impact on others than mere words—'yad yad acarati sresthas tat tad evatero janah' (Gita 3.21). When human beings perform their respective duties, it influences the devas as well, prompting them to fulfill their duties and bring rain (Gita 3.11). In this context, there is a story: There were four young peasant boys. Even when the month of Ashadha arrived, there was no rain. They reasoned: 'It is time to plow the fields; even if rain hasn't fallen, let us fulfill our duty on time.' Thinking thus, they went to the fields and started plowing. Seeing them plow, peacocks thought: 'Rain hasn't fallen yet, why are they plowing?' Upon learning that the boys were performing their duty, the peacocks thought...

'Karma brahmodbhavam viddhi'—the Vedas describe the method of performing duty-bound actions (Gita 4.32). Because humans acquire knowledge of how to perform duties from the Vedas, actions are said to originate from the Vedas.

'Brahmaaksarasamudbhavam'—Here the word 'Brahma' signifies the Vedas. The Vedas originated from the Supreme Lord of Sacchidananda (Gita 17.23). Thus, the Lord is the root of all. From the Lord originate the Vedas. The Vedas describe the method of performing duty. Human beings perform that duty according to scriptural ordinance. Through the performance of duty-bound actions, Yajna arises, and from Yajna comes rain. Rain produces food, food sustains creatures, and among those creatures, humans perform Yajna by discharging their duties*. Thus this cosmic wheel keeps revolving.

'Tasmat sarva-gatam brahma nityam yajne pratisthitam'—Here the word 'Brahma' refers to the Imperishable (saguna-nirakara Supreme Being). Therefore, the Supreme Being is all-pervading (sarva-gata), not the Vedas. Even though all-pervading, the Supreme Being is ever-present in a special manner within 'Yajna' (duty-bound action). The meaning is that wherever duty is performed with a desireless attitude, God resides there. Therefore, human beings seeking God-realization can easily attain Him through their duties—'svakarmana tam abhyarcya siddhim vindati manavah' (Gita 18.46).

197

Question—If God is all-pervading, why is He said to be eternally established specifically in Yajna? Is He not eternally established elsewhere?

Answer—God is indeed eternally present equally everywhere. He is neither temporary nor localized. That is why He is called 'sarva-gata' (all-pervading) here. Saying He is eternally established in Yajna (duty) implies that Yajna is the locus of His realization. Even though water is present everywhere beneath the ground, it is accessible through a well, not everywhere. Even though water is present throughout a pipe, it is obtained only where there is a tap or opening. Similarly, though all-pervading, God is realized through Yajna.

By acting for oneself and assuming a relationship with inert matter (body, etc.), an obstacle (veil) arises in realizing the all-pervading God. By performing one's duty selflessly solely for the benefit of others, this obstacle is removed, and the ever-attained God is naturally realized. This is why the Lord is placing special emphasis on performing duty through various arguments to Arjuna, who wished to shrink from his duty.

Context—The responsibility of moving according to the cosmic wheel—that is, performing one's duty—rests solely upon human beings. Therefore, the Lord reprimands in the following verse the person who does not perform his duty.

Evam pravartitam cakram nanuvartayatiha yah |
Aghayur indriyaramo mogham partha sa jivati || 16 ||

partha = O son of Kunti (Partha)!
yah = a person who
iha = in this world
evam = in this manner
pravartitam = set in motion (from tradition)
cakram = cosmic wheel
na, anuvartayati = does not follow,
sah = he
indriyarama = delighting in sense pleasures through senses
aghayuh = leads a sinful life (aghayu)
manusyah = human being
mogham = in vain
jivati = lives.

Commentary——'Partha'—Concluding the section begun in verse 9, the Lord addresses Arjuna as 'Partha', as if saying: "You are the son of that very Pritha (Kunti), who endured lifelong hardships yet fulfilled her duty. Therefore, neglect of duty should not come from you either. The battle which you call a dreadful act is not a dreadful act for you, but rather a Yajna (duty). Fulfilling it is acting in accordance with the cosmic wheel, and failing to fulfill it is acting contrary to the cosmic wheel."

* Through all non-human stationary and moving creatures, Yajna (welfare of others) happens naturally, but they cannot perform Yajna consciously. Only human beings can consciously perform Yajna, because humans alone possess the capability and right for it.

'Evam pravartitam cakram nanuvartayatiha yah'—just as when even a small part of a chariot wheel breaks, a severe jolt affects all parts of the chariot along with the rider and charioteer; similarly, a person who does not live in harmony with the cosmic wheel described in verses 14 and 15 creates an obstacle in the operation of the entire creation.

The world and the individual are not two alien entities. Just as there is an intimate relationship between the body and its limbs, so there is an intimate bond between the world and the individual. When an individual abandons desire, mine-ness, attachment, and egoism to perform their duty, happiness naturally flows to all creation.

'Indriyaramah'—a person who, possessed of desire, mine-ness, and attachment, indulges in sense pleasures through their senses is called here 'one who delights in sense pleasures'. Such a person is lower even than an animal; because an animal does not commit new sins, but rather moves toward purity by merely exhausting the fruits of past sins. In contrast, an 'indriyaraam' (sense-delighter) person commits new sins leading to moral downfall, and by disrupting the cosmic wheel, inflicts suffering on the entire universe.

'Aghayuh'—the life of a person who does not live in harmony with the cosmic wheel is purely sinful. This is because a person who indulges in sense enjoyment with a pleasure-seeking attitude cannot escape the sin of harm/violence. A selfish, arrogant person seeking luxury and accumulation harms others; therefore, their life is inherently sinful.

Goswami Tulsidas Ji says:
'Par drohi par dar rata par dhana par apabada |
Te nara pamvara papamaya deha dharem manujada ||' (Ramcharitmanas 7.39)
"Those men who harm others, covet others' wives, steal others' wealth, and slander others are wretched, sinful demons in human form."

'Mogham partha sa jivati'—censuring and reprimanding the person who fails to do his duty in refined language, the Lord says that such a person lives in vain in this world—meaning it were better if he died! The implication is that if he cannot bring happiness to creation by performing his duty, he should at least not cause distress. Just as during Lord Rama's exile, when the residents of Ayodhya visited Chitrakoot, the forest dwellers (Kols, Kirats, Bhils) told them: "That we do not steal your clothes and utensils is our greatest service to you" (Ramcharitmanas 2.251.2); similarly, if those who do not perform their duty refrain at least from disrupting the cosmic wheel, that itself is their service.

Regarding a person who does not align with the cosmic wheel, the Lord earlier stated: 'stena eva sah' (Gita 3.12), "he is indeed a thief", and 'bhunjate te tv agham' (Gita 3.13), "they eat only sin"; and now in this verse, calling him 'aghayur indriyarama' ("sinful in life and delighting in senses"), He declares his very living to be futile.

Goswami Tulsidas Ji Maharaj has also said:
'Teja krisanu rosa mahisesa | Agha avaguna dhana dhani dhanesa ||
Udaya keta sama hita sabahike | Kumbhakarana sama sovata nike ||' (Ramcharitmanas 1.4.3)

Commentary——'Yastvatmaratir eva .... ca santustas tasya'—Here the word 'tu' (but) is used to highlight the extraordinary distinction of a great soul who has attained perfection through selfless action compared to the person described in the previous verse who fails to perform his duty.

As long as a person regards his relationship with the world as real, he considers his 'rati' (delight/love) to lie in sense pleasures and in wife, children, family, etc., his 'tripti' (satisfaction) in food and water, and his 'santusti' (contentment) in wealth. However, in these things, his delight, satisfaction, and contentment are neither ever complete nor ever continuous. This is because the world changes every moment, is inert, and perishable; whereas the 'Self' is ever uniform, conscious, and imperishable. The point is that the 'Self' has not even the slightest connection with the world. Therefore, how could the Self's delight, satisfaction, and contentment ever come from the world?

No person's love for the world remains forever—this is everyone's lived experience. The mutual love or attraction felt between husband and wife at the time of marriage wanes after having one or two children. In some cases, women even remark about their elderly husband: "It would be better if the old man died!" The satisfaction derived from eating food lasts only for a short time; the contentment a person feels upon acquiring wealth is also fleeting, because the greed for wealth keeps growing continuously. Thus, a deficiency always persists. The essence is that delight, satisfaction, and contentment can never remain permanent in the world. Human beings merely perceive an illusion of delight, satisfaction, and contentment in worldly objects, but it does not truly exist; if it did, disinterest, dissatisfaction, and discontentment would never arise again. By essential nature, delight, satisfaction, and contentment are self-evident. The Self is Existence (Sat). In Sat, there is never any non-existence—'na bhavo vidyate satah' (Gita 2.16); and without deficiency, no desire arises. Therefore, desirelessness in the Self is self-evident. But when the individual soul mistakenly considers its relationship with the world as real, it begins searching for delight, satisfaction, and contentment in the world, desiring worldly objects for this purpose. After desiring, when that object (wealth, etc.) is obtained, once the existing desire leaves the mind (before a new desire is born), one's state becomes desireless, and one experiences the joy of that desirelessness. However, by mistake, a person attributes that joy to the acquisition of the worldly object and calls that joy by the names of delight, satisfaction, and contentment. If that joy came from acquiring the object, then after receiving it, as long as the object remained, joy would persist forever, sorrow would never occur, and desire for objects would not arise again. But because complete (eternal) delight, satisfaction, and contentment can never be gained from worldly objects, and because attachment to the world persists, one begins making new desires again. When desire arises, one feels deficiency; and when the desired object is attained, one feels dependence. Therefore, a person filled with desire is ever miserable.

It is worth noting here that spiritual seekers consider desirelessness to be the root cause of happiness and desire to be the cause of sorrow; whereas worldly attached people consider acquiring objects to be happiness and non-acquisition to be sorrow. If an attached person were also to view reality with true insight like a seeker, they could quickly experience self-evident desirelessness.

Desire-bound persons are declared eligible for Karmayoga—'karmayogastu kaminam' (Shrimad Bhagavatam 11.20.7). The delight, satisfaction, and contentment of desire-bound persons lie in the world. Therefore, describing the state of selfless great souls perfected through Karmayoga, the Lord states that their delight, satisfaction, and contentment do not lie in the world like desire-bound persons, but in their own Self (Gita 2.55), which is already present by essential nature.

Enduring cheerfully whatever hardship or adverse circumstance naturally arises while fulfilling one's duty is called 'tapas' (austerity). Without tapas, purity does not enter the inner conscience (antahkarana), and without purity, sublime truths cannot be assimilated. Therefore, the Lord says that this most confidential secret should not be told to one who is not austere.

One who is not tolerant/forbearing is also non-austere. Therefore, this most secret truth should not be told to such a person either. This tolerance is of four kinds:
(1) Dvandva-sahisnuta (Tolerance of Duality)—Becoming free from dualities like attraction-aversion, joy-sorrow, pleasure-pain, honor-dishonor, praise-blame—'te dvandva-moha-nirmuktah' (Gita 7.28); 'dvandvair vimuktah sukha-duhkha-samjnaih' (Gita 15.5).
(2) Vega-sahisnuta (Tolerance of Impulses)—Not allowing impulses of lust, anger, greed, malice, etc., to arise—'kama-krodhodbhavam vegam' (Gita 5.23).
(3) Paramata-sahisnuta (Tolerance of Others' Views)—Hearing the glory of others' viewpoints without doubting one's own path and without getting agitated by their views*—'ekam sankhyam ca yogam ca yah pasyati sa pasyati' (Gita 5.5).
(4) Parotkarsa-sahisnuta (Tolerance of Others' Excellence)—Though lacking in competence, authority, status, renunciation, or penance oneself, remaining completely untroubled upon hearing praise of others' competence, authority, etc.—'vimatsarah' (Gita 4.22); 'harsamarsa-bhayodvegair muktah' (Gita 12.15).

* Having mutual differences of opinion and practicing spiritual discipline according to one's own path is not a fault; rather, disliking others' views, refuting their doctrines, or harboring hatred toward their path is the real fault.
